Did the invention of nuclear weapons ultimately make the world a safer place?

I would say that it's too soon to say.

You could say that the massive power and expense of nuclear weapons has given rise to the modern superpower and changed the nature of international conflict. But, I think we'd be hard pressed to demonstrate a significant change in "safety" (we need to define that term- likelihood of individuals to die in violence? Or frequency/scale of nation-state level conflicts? Or simple maintenance of the status-quo?) with only about 70 years of data.

All again in another 100 years, or after the second time a a nuclear device is used in a conflict, possibly including terrorist action, whichever comes first. (Yes, I'm picking 170 years pretty arbitrarily we should ask a historian how long these things take to fully develop and for us to understand)

I would say that no, nuclear weapons haven't made the world a safer place. The number of detonations for "testing" is huge.

Medically and physically, the number of detonations for "testing" is huge. I personally believe that the number of detonations and increase in background radioactivity since the 1940's is the largest part of why people are being diagnosed with cancer. I know that improved diagnostics mean that it is detected more often and earlier in the onset than before So that could also explain increased diagnoses. Radioactive exposure alters cellular activity and genetic mutations are increased in cells exposed to radiation. It has had a global impact, that we just haven't seen long term effects of as yet.

Mental illness is also strongly tied to radioactive exposure, but whether that is a symptom of radiation or the usually traumatic events around being exposed to radiation, is unclear.

As for the sociopolitical impacts, no I don't believe they have made the world safer. Sure, dropping two big ass nuclear mofo's on Japan ended the second world war, but tensions around the globe haven't abated. If anything, they have become more extreme and expensive - human lives lost and economic costs are exponentially spiralling out of control.

Pakistan and India are the forgotten nuclear powers. Pakistan has proven itself to be an unworthy, deceitful player in middle eastern conflict. There is a reason that the "war" on the Taliban failed, and it is because of the double dealings of Pakistan's IS. Remember, this is a country run by thugs who believe it's okay to shoot a girl child in the head for daring to go to school. And she was just the one we heard about. I don't like that Pakistan has any weaponry remotely nuclear.

As for Israel & Iran, what can be said? So many human rights abuses. All arising from a few pencil marks made by cowardly fleeing colonists who have become immeasurably wealthy from the costs of those countries and their aggressions against other nation states.

There are currently over 42 Active Conflicts Globally - which is relatively low historically speaking. Live global conflict tracker:

Why this number is dropping is a complex thing. I haven't researched enough of it yet to speak on it, but would hazard a guess that there are bigger issues within nation states than internationally.

TL:DR; Nope, I don't think nuclear weaponry has made the world safer.

Has Capitalism done more to reduce absolute poverty than any form of Socialism ever implemented?

Frankly, I don't understand why people think capitalism and socialism are somehow exclusive ideas. I view property ownership, business ownership, healthcare, and education all as basic human rights. A "social-capitalist" society, if you will, would be ideal if you're looking to minimize poverty and the societal rot that it invites.

I have been coming around to this point of view, ever since I started reading about basic minimum incomes. The idea that you can provide everyone a minimum standard of living without out killing work incentives is appealing. I'm not completely convinced yet but it's an interesting topic. How do you believe a "social-capitalist" society should be structured? I am also concerned about creep in either direction what kind of mechanisms could identify and maintain balance?

I think that basic minimum income is a really inelegant solution. I'm not sure if I know of a better one, but I think it's much more fair and much more simple to remove the burden of cost from things that are essential to the basic standard of living. Public transit subsidies, produce subsidies, free healthcare, free education, alternate energy incentives, alternate transport incentives, etc, etc. I think the government actually governing to help produce a healthy, intelligent, environmentally conscious society would do more for poverty than trying to "make it rain" by taking bills directly out of rich people's pockets and sliding them into the pockets of the poor. The whole reason for government is that it's easier to implement growth with preexisting infrastructure, but that's not being taken advantage of in our current system. We live in a capitalist society, but our government is also capitalistic, which is flawed.
